title: Circuit breakers, bulkheads, rate limiters and graceful degradation
seriesDescription: Language-independent interview topics (concepts, SQL, design, AI engineering): no Java and no Python code or library names.
description: The circuit-breaker state machine and its thresholds, token-bucket arithmetic, bulkhead sizing with Little's law, rate-limit responses and designing safe fallbacks.
source: Martin Fowler (CircuitBreaker); Release It! (Nygard); Google SRE Book (Handling Overload); Stripe engineering blog on rate limiters; nginx ngx_http_limit_req_module documentation

questions.prompt: Match each circuit-breaker state with its behaviour.

right.text: Calls pass through and failures are counted
Calls are rejected immediately without contacting the dependency
A limited number of trial calls decide whether to close or reopen
Calls are queued until the dependency recovers

questions.explanation: CLOSED to OPEN when the failure (or slow-call) rate crosses the threshold; OPEN to HALF_OPEN after the wait duration; HALF_OPEN to CLOSED if trial calls succeed, else back to OPEN.

questions.prompt: A count-based breaker has a window of 10 calls, a minimum of 10 calls before it evaluates, and a failure-rate threshold of 50 percent. After 10 calls, what is the smallest number of failed calls that opens the circuit?
questions.explanation: The breaker opens when the failure rate is greater than or equal to the threshold: 5 of 10 is 50 percent. Fewer than the minimum number of calls never opens it.

questions.prompt: A breaker is HALF_OPEN with 4 permitted trial calls and a failure-rate threshold of 50 percent. After the 4 trial calls, what is the largest number of failed trials for which the breaker still returns to CLOSED?
questions.explanation: The breaker opens when the failure rate is greater than or equal to the threshold. 1 of 4 is 25 percent (closes), 2 of 4 is 50 percent (reopens), so at most 1.

questions.prompt: A token bucket has capacity 10 and refills 2 tokens per second, and starts full. At t = 0 ten requests arrive and are all served. At t = 4 s, nine requests arrive at once. How many are served?
questions.explanation: The bucket was empty at t = 0 and refills 2 x 4 = 8 tokens by t = 4 (below the cap of 10), so 8 of the 9 are served and 1 is rejected.

questions.prompt: A bulkhead allows at most 10 concurrent calls to a dependency and each call takes 200 ms. By Little's law, what is the maximum throughput to that dependency in requests per second?
questions.explanation: Throughput = concurrency / latency = 10 / 0.2 = 50 per second. If latency rises to 1 s, the same bulkhead only allows 10 per second, which is the protective point.

questions.prompt: Match each rate-limiting algorithm with its characteristic.

right.text: Allows bursts up to the bucket size, then a steady refill rate
Smooths traffic to a constant outflow rate
Cheap but a client can send double the limit across a window boundary
Stores a timestamp per request, exact but memory heavy
Blocks every request after the first failure

questions.explanation: Fixed-window boundary burst: with 100 per minute, 100 requests at 0:59 and 100 at 1:01 make 200 in two seconds. Sliding window counters approximate the log cheaply.

questions.prompt: Write the nginx configuration that defines a 10 MB shared zone named api keyed by client address allowing 5 requests per second, and applies it with a burst of 10 inside location /search.

checks.label: defines the zone with the client address key

questions.explanation: limit_req_zone belongs in the http block. Without nodelay, burst requests are queued and released at the zone rate; with it they pass immediately and later ones are rejected (503 by default, 429 with limit_req_status 429).

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: A circuit breaker protects both the caller and a struggling dependency.
questions.reason: While the circuit is open, calls fail immediately instead of consuming caller threads and adding load to the dependency.

whys.a: Correct: Failing fast frees the caller's resources and gives the dependency room to recover.
whys.b: Not this one: Both are true but R is not the reason A holds does not describe this pair; R is actually the reason or is false.
whys.c: Not this one: A is true while R is false does not describe this pair; check the truth of R again.
whys.d: Not this one: A is false while R is true does not describe this pair; check the truth of A again.

questions.explanation: Pair the breaker with timeouts; without timeouts a breaker never sees a failure from a hung call.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: A token bucket permits a short burst of requests up to its capacity.
questions.reason: A leaky bucket sends requests to the backend at a constant rate.

whys.a: Not this one: Both A and R are true and R explains A does not describe this pair; R does not explain A.
whys.b: Correct: Both are true, but the leaky bucket property is a different algorithm and does not explain the token-bucket burst.
whys.c: Not this one: A is true while R is false does not describe this pair; check the truth of R again.
whys.d: Not this one: A is false while R is true does not describe this pair; check the truth of A again.

questions.explanation: Token bucket: bursty but bounded average. Leaky bucket: smooth output, queued excess. Stripe uses token buckets for request limiting.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: Rate limiting by API key rather than with one global limit stops a single noisy tenant from starving the others.
questions.reason: A single global limit treats every client separately, so it protects each of them equally.

whys.a: Not this one: Both A and R are true and R explains A does not describe this pair; R does not explain A.
whys.b: Not this one: Both are true but R is not the reason A holds does not describe this pair; R is actually the reason or is false.
whys.c: Correct: A is true. R is false: a single global limit is shared, so one noisy client can consume it all.
whys.d: Not this one: A is false while R is true does not describe this pair; check the truth of A again.

questions.explanation: Use layered limits: per key, per IP, per endpoint, plus a global safety limit and load shedding.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: In the HALF_OPEN state a circuit breaker lets all traffic through to test whether the dependency has recovered.
questions.reason: HALF_OPEN permits only a configured number of trial calls and decides to close or reopen from their results.

whys.a: Not this one: Both A and R are true and R explains A does not describe this pair; R does not explain A.
whys.b: Not this one: Both are true but R is not the reason A holds does not describe this pair; R is actually the reason or is false.
whys.c: Not this one: A is true while R is false does not describe this pair; check the truth of R again.
whys.d: Correct: A is false: only a limited number of trial calls pass. R is true.

questions.explanation: Letting everyone through at once could knock the recovering service over again.

questions.text: When a dependency fails, return a {1} such as cached data, hide non-critical {2} behind flags, and use load {3} to drop low-priority requests under overload.
questions.explanation: Degrade in layers from stale data to reduced features to explicit errors, and tell the client when data is stale.

questions.prompt: Which are sound degradation strategies when a dependency is down? Select all that apply.

options.text: Serve the last known recommendations from cache and mark them stale.
options.why: Correct: useful, honest and low risk.

options.text: Hide the reviews widget while the reviews service is unavailable.
options.why: Correct: a non-critical feature can disappear without breaking checkout.

options.text: Queue the confirmation email and send it when the mail service returns.
options.why: Correct: the work is deferred, not lost.

options.text: Report a payment as successful when the gateway cannot be reached.
options.why: This invents a business outcome and loses money or trust.

options.text: Return an empty 200 for a failed balance lookup, with no signal.
options.why: A silent empty answer looks like a real zero balance.

questions.explanation: A good fallback is honest, safe for the business, and observable (metric and log every fallback so you notice).

questions.prompt: A service must tell a client that exceeded its rate limit to slow down. Which response is the standard way?

options.text: HTTP 200 with an error message in the response body, hiding the failure.
options.why: A success status hides the failure from clients, proxies and monitoring.

options.text: HTTP 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header.
options.why: Correct: 429 is the status defined for rate limiting.

options.text: HTTP 404 Not Found, to make the endpoint look absent to the caller.
options.why: A missing-resource status misleads clients and may be cached.

options.text: HTTP 500 with no further hint, so that clients retry again very soon.
options.why: A server error without guidance invites immediate retries.

questions.explanation: Use 429 for per-client limits and 503 (also with Retry-After) when the whole service sheds load. Well-behaved clients honour Retry-After and add jitter.

questions.prompt: True or false: a circuit breaker will open on its own when a dependency hangs forever, even if the calls have no timeout.

options.why: A hung call never completes, so the breaker never records a failure.
Correct: failures are only counted when a call returns or times out.

questions.explanation: Always set a timeout on the guarded call; a slow-call threshold also lets the breaker trip on latency, but it still needs the call to finish.

questions.prompt: A service can handle 800 requests per second but receives 1,000. If it sheds the excess at the front door, what percentage of the traffic is rejected?
questions.explanation: 200 of 1,000 requests are rejected: 20 percent. Shedding early keeps latency good for the admitted 80 percent; accepting everything would grow queues until all requests time out.
